newsitem.title: UK: U.S. should rethink Colombia policy, VP says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. should rethink Colombia policy, VP says.

text.p: Colombia's new vice president said on Tuesday a landmark law aimed at bankrupting the nation's billionaire drug barons should make the United States rethink its policy towards the Latin American country.
Carlos Lemos Simmonds said in a Reuters interview Colombia would reap huge benefits from the new measure, but added that Washington should also look to its own backyard in its war against narcotics.

"If the United States were doing one half of what we are doing to stop production the situation would be very different," said Lemos, who was elected vice president in September but remains in London as Colombia's ambassador to Britain.
"I would like to see a law like the one we have in Colombia now (being implemented) in the United States," he added.
On Thursday Colombia's congress overwhelmingly approved a forfeiture law entailing the retroactive seizure of illicit gains made by drug lords over the past 20 years.
The hope in Bogota is that this will persuade Washington to reverse its decision to decertify the nation as a partner in its anti-drug war, and lift the threat of trade sanctions next year.

"If the U.S. officials in charge are objective they should withdraw their decertification of Colombia because there is enough proof of how the country, the government and the president himself are fighting drug dealers," Lemos said.

And he warned that isolating Colombia, fighting a dual battle against drug kings and left-wing guerrillas who are increasingly making common cause, could set a dangerous precedent across Latin America.
"It is very dangerous to push Colombia too hard, because it may play into the hands of the guerrilla movements," he said.

"If the link between guerrillas and drug lords succeeds in Colombia we are going to have many similar cases over the whole continent," he added, pointing to potentially similar situations in Mexico and Central America.
"To overcome these problems we need international cooperation, not international sanctions," he added.

Early estimates value the narco-traffickers' total assets at $500 million, he said. They can be seized as soon as President Ernesto Samper signs Thursday's bill into law, probably this week, and the proceeds will benefit the nation.

"There will be a huge distribution of assets in Colombia as a consequence of this law," he said. "The best lands in the country will be given to poor farmers, the country houses will be gIven to poor children and the elderly, and the artworks will go to museums."

Bogota is having to divert money from infrastructure projects and make wealthy citizens buy so-called war bonds to fund its anti-drug fight when most Latin American governments are slashing their defence budgets.
Investors are worried this will dent Colombia's sturdy GDP growth, which has helped make it one of only two Latin American nations to have the kudos of an investment grade credit rating.
Lemos said the United States should tackle the huge demand for drugs inside its own borders which is keeping the international drug market alive.

"Now is the time the United States should think seriously about demand -- they have punished Colombia, they will punish other countries, but that is just a pretext for not thinking about demand (at home)," he said, comparing Colombia's $2 billion drug trade with an industry in the U.S. worth $70 billion.

A low-profile vice president, Lemos said he was happy to remain in London to further Colombia's international agenda and has no desire to haggle for the country's top job. He would be expected to become president if Samper ever chose to resign.
"I certainly hope that will not happen," he said. "I pray every day for the health of President Samper."
